packages.label: הַצַּדִּיק וְהַחַיִּים
packages.reason: This cluster groups all concepts that share the essential nature of 'the one who controls his desire and therefore is always alive.' The teaching's central bechina declaration is: the Tzaddik is never dead — he is תָּמִיד חַי (always alive), even after physical death. This is because for him, life consists in serving God (עֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם), which continues uninterrupted beyond the grave. The text further defines the Tzaddik's quality: he כּוֹבֵשׁ אֶת יִצְרוֹ (subdues his inclination) and אוֹחֵז אֶת תַּאֲוָתוֹ בְּיָדוֹ (holds his desire in his hand) — even regarding the permitted half (חֶצְיוֹ לָכֶם), he maintains mastery. These three dimensions — Tzaddik, life/always-alive, and the subduing of desire — all express the same essential reality: the axis of holiness and spiritual vitality that transcends death. The explicit bechina marker is the statement 'בְּוַדַּאי זֶה אֵין מֵת, אֶלָּא תָּמִיד חַי' — this person IS not dead, IS always alive. This IS-language equates the Tzaddik's type with the concept of enduring life. The axis of this package is: Tzaddik = control of desire = life. Polarity is good — this is the positive pole of the teaching.

packages.label: תַּאֲוַת אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה וְהַמָּוֶת
packages.label_en: Desires of Eating and Drinking and Death
packages.reason: This cluster groups all concepts that share the essential nature of 'being enslaved to physical desire, which constitutes a form of death.' The teaching's most explicit bechina statement is: 'זֶה נִקְרָא מֵת' — the person who followed desires of eating and drinking all his days IS CALLED (נִקְרָא) dead. The word נִקְרָא is one of the canonical bechina markers in the framework ('X נִקְרָא Y — X is called Y'). The equation made here is: the desire-chaser = מֵת (the dead). After physical death his lack of eating/drinking shows that death has occurred — death is recognizable (נִכֶּרֶת) in him, because his entire identity was eating and drinking, and now that is gone. The two concepts in this package — תַּאֲווֹת אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה (desires of eating and drinking) and מֵת (the dead / death) — share the same essential nature: both represent existence without inner life, without transcendence, without the axis that connects a person to God. The desire is the death-orientation expressed in life; the death is the desire-orientation made manifest. This is not a causal chain (desires do not 'produce' death as an eitza mechanism in this text) — rather, the Rebbe is saying they ARE the same thing: to live for desire IS death. Polarity is evil — this is the negative pole of the teaching, the anti-life axis.
